transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Ava Reed (Redwood AE); Samir Patel (Redwood SE); Diego Morales (Redwood Solutions Eng); Lena Cho (NovaAI CTO); Marco Ruiz (NovaAI Platform/DevOps); Priya Nair (NovaAI Security); Jonas Berg (NovaAI Product)

Summary:
Quick demo and architecture review for tenant key strategy. Walked through org vs project key tradeoffs, adaptive rate/quotas, sticky routing for stateful KV-cache sessions, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quant profiles. Customer had questions about VPC/private deployment, SOC2, and how throttles affect latency-sensitive inference. Agreed next steps to share security docs and run a pilot.

Topics covered: org/project key mapping, fair-burst patterns, concurrency quotas, token-level throttles, Console demo: quota UI + routing rules, API examples, Optimize suggestions for request shaping.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Reed: alright everyone, thanks for joining on time so we'll get started. I'm Ava, AE on the account, with Samir and Diego from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Lena Cho: doing good, thanks. we've got a short window so appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:12] Marco Ruiz: hi all. we're mainly focused on how to prevent noisy tenants from impacting latency for our realtime routes.
[00:18] Ava: perfect, that's exactly what we planned to show — key strategies, quotas, and some routing examples in the Console. Samir do you want to kick off with the high level?
[00:25] Samir Patel: yeah sure; quick context — Redwood's common pattern is to use an "org key" to represent the customer org and then issue "project keys" per product or team, so you can put quotas and routing policy at either level. the demo will show how you can set fair-burst, concurrency limits, and sticky routing for k-v cache heavy flows. note: i'm gonna say 'kay-vee cache' a couple times cause the transcript might pick it up odd.
[00:46] Jonas Berg: quick question, do you recommend org keys for billing isolation or project keys?
[00:50] Samir: depends — org keys are great for global limits and billing; project keys give you per-product quotas and make isolating noisy teams much easier. many customers use a hybrid: org-level spend cap plus per-project concurrency and token throttles.
[01:07] Priya Nair: security lens: how does data residency and VPC private control work with project keys? if we put a project key on a private subnet will the logs still flow to Redwood console?
[01:17] Diego Morales: yes — private deployments (VPC) keep inference within your network and you get a control-plane link for metrics and audit logs; logs are pushed via an encrypted channel, and you can opt to keep long-term logs on your side. we'll send the exact flow diagram after.
[01:33] Lena: okay good. and compliance — SOC2?
[01:36] Ava: SOC2 plus our KMS integrations and HSM options for private deployment — we'll include SOC2 report and SAML + SSO setup docs in the follow-up.
[01:44] [02:00] Samir: jumping into Console — screen share here. I'm opening the org page, you can see default quotas: per-minute tokens, concurrency slots, and per-key burst window.
[02:10] Samir: so here's a common policy: org overall TPS cap 500, but then projects get slices — project A gets 300, B gets 150, C gets 50. if A exceeds its share and B is idle, we can allow fair-burst to borrow up to X% of unused org capacity, or we can restrict to strict slicing.
[02:30] Marco: do you support sticky routing for sessions that need KV cache hotness? if a request moves between cells the kv cache warms cold and latency spikes.
[02:36] Samir: yes; we have affinity rules. you can mark a route as sticky, and requests from the same project key will be routed to the same serving pool when possible. fallback exists if that pool is overloaded — automatic reroute to a compatible quantized variant.
[02:53] [03:20] Ava: want to show the API examples — Diego?
[03:23] Diego: sure — example curl: POST to /v1/generate with header x-redwood-key: project_xxx. we showed rate headers in the response: x-rw-remaining, x-rw-limit, x-rw-reset which clients can use to implement graceful backoff. note sometimes the header names get altered in proxies so watch for that.
[03:44] Marco: cool, that helps. what's the behavior when token throttles kick in mid-generation? we have some 1–2s tail latency targets.
[03:52] Samir: by default we return a 429 once a token budget is hit. for streaming calls there's also a partial-complete with a warning header option — you can choose automatic queuing with a max wait TTL, or immediate rejection. queuing increases latency but preserves throughput; immediate 429s let your app fail-fast.
[04:12] Lena: hmm, queuing worries me because it could add unpredictability for our real-time chat.
[04:16] Ava: totally, many realtime apps prefer strict concurrency quotas and small per-request token limits to avoid long queue waits. Optimize can analyze your traffic and recommend a profile that balances cost and tail latency.
[04:28] [05:00] Samir: switching to Optimize — here's a quick run: we fed a sample of NovaAI's typical prompts and Optimize suggested batching window 25–40ms for answer size under 512 tokens, and quantization profile q4_8 for non-LLM-critical routes; it flagged some prompts that are brittle to quantization so keep those on the higher-fidelity model.
[05:22] Jonas: that quant recommendation — is it automated or you run it with us?
[05:25] Diego: we can run an automated job or perform a consultative review. for pilots we usually do an initial sweep and then iterate once we have more traces.
[05:33] [06:00] Marco: can routing rules be time-based? e.g., daytime strict, night relaxed for batch processing?
[06:04] Samir: yes, scheduling is first-class in routing rules. you can have policies that change quotas and preferred model variants by time-of-day or by traffic volume thresholds.
[06:12] Priya: encryption-in-transit and at-rest— if we keep logs on our side, can we still get the same error tracing?
[06:17] Diego: you get trace IDs and sampling information forwarded; you can keep detailed logs on your side while sending anonymized metrics to Redwood. there's also an option for encrypted blobs for offline debugging.
[06:35] [07:00] Ava: ok let's do a small hypothetical — Nova runs a realtime assistant, product route R1 is latency sensitive, batch job B2 is tolerant. how would you carve keys and quotas?
[07:09] Samir: carve it like this: org-level spend cap plus dedicated project key R1 with concurrency 20, token cap per-min 10k, no queuing; B2 gets project key with high token cap and looser concurrency but allowed to burst into unused org capacity during off-hours. set routing to pin R1 to low-latency pool.
[07:30] Lena: and for multi-tenant customers of Nova? we are multi-tenant inside R1 — how do we avoid one tenant inside R1 bringing the whole route down?
[07:37] Samir: you can subdivide within project keys by issuing sub-keys per tenant, or implement soft-rate-limits at application layer and enforce hard token quotas at the project subkey level. another approach is fairshare across subkeys to avoid single-tenant storms.
[07:54] [08:20] Marco: what's the monitoring resolution? we need minute-level alerting on 95th pct latency and throttle events.
[08:25] Diego: Console exposes per-key and per-route dashboards with 1m granularity by default, and you can set alerts on 95th, errors, and 429 spikes. traces link to sample requests for diagnostics.
[08:40] [09:00] Samir: showing demo of setting a policy — I'm creating a concurrency quota and a token window, then attaching to project key 'R1-prod'. now demonstrating a fair-burst rule: allow 20% borrow from unused org capacity but cap single tenant borrow to 10% so no single tenant can borrow the whole thing.
[09:22] Priya: that per-tenant borrow cap is helpful. is that enforced at the control plane or at the serving runtime?
[09:30] Samir: enforced in the serving runtime — it's part of the request admission pipeline. control plane pushes the policy down and runtime enforces it locally for pod-level admission.
[09:45] [10:00] Ava: quick note: when we say 'borrowing', it can be enabled or disabled per org; some customers prefer strict slices only.
[10:06] [10:30] Marco: what about peak protection when a single customer goes from 0 to huge in 30s — can we do cold-start prevention?
[10:35] Samir: yes, guardrails like warm-warm pools and burst buckets allow short spikes without eviction. we also offer burst tokens with decay windows to allow one-off spikes but not sustained abuse.
[10:50] [11:20] Diego: I'm going to run a quick simulated load to show how throttles behave — starting a synthetic client sending requests with project_xxx key.
[11:25] [11:50] Diego: you can see in the Console the live throttle events — red markers — and the client gets 429s when the per-key token budget is exhausted. streaming calls show partial output and a 429 at the end in this config.
[12:05] Marco: can the client see remaining tokens to pace themselves?
[12:09] Diego: yes those x-rw-* headers. we also recommend the SDK which exposes a token budget API for adaptive backoff.
[12:20] [12:45] Lena: what's support for canary or staged rollout if we change quotas? we don't want a quota change to silently kill traffic.
[12:51] Samir: our console supports staged rollout and canary for quota changes: you can apply a change to a subset of projects or a percent of traffic and monitor before wider roll-out. automatic fallback policies are available if error rates increase.
[13:05] [13:40] Priya: SOC2 and audit logs — we need logs for every quota-change event including who made the change.
[13:46] Ava: we emit audit events with actor, timestamp, and diff. in private deployment you can pipe raw audit events to your SIEM. we'll attach a sample audit export.
[14:00] [14:30] Jonas: question about multi-region routing — if we pin a project to a region for data residency how do you handle failover?
[14:36] Samir: you can set primary-region affinity with an automated cross-region fallback; in the event of regional capacity loss we failover to the nearest compatible region but only after configured health checks. this preserves residency under normal ops and still gives resilience.
[14:55] [15:20] Diego: showing the Optimize report again — it simulated cost vs latency tradeoffs; here's a slider we use in the Console to visualize cost per thousand tokens vs 95th latency for different quant profiles.
[15:35] Marco: helpful. one operational question: is there a way to automatically throttle only background batch jobs first rather than realtime ones during outage?
[15:42] Samir: yes, priority classes exist. you can tag routes as realtime or batch and set eviction/queueing preference so batch traffic yields first.
[15:55] [16:20] Ava: let's discuss pilot scope — Samir, what do we need to validate for Nova?
[16:25] Samir: pilot scope: 1) run a traffic replay for peak hour and measure 95th latency under queued and strict policies, 2) test sticky routing with kv-heavy sessions, 3) validate audit and SSO integration. estimated 2 weeks.
[16:40] Marco: for replay we can share anonymized traces. what's the minimal infra we need for pilot?
[16:45] Diego: usually a small dedicated pool (2–4 GPUs) and access to a control-plane integration; private pilot can be VPC peered. we'll include the infra footprint in the follow-up.
[16:58] [17:30] Priya: are there any gotchas for SAML + Okta? we've had issues before where SSO broke automation keys.
[17:36] Ava: common: service account keys must be independent of interactive SSO; we have best-practices doc — we'll include sample SAML assertion mapping to roles.
[17:50] [18:10] Diego: also note that token rotation is supported; project keys can be rotated without downtime if you pre-load the new keys and then switch traffic.
[18:20] Jonas: how do you charge for dedicated capacity in a pilot?
[18:24] Ava: for pilots we often do a short-term dedicated commit or a credit-backed usage model; we'll put options in the pricing note.
[18:33] [19:00] Marco: anything else on throttling semantics? are there 'soft' throttles that log but don't block?
[19:06] Samir: yes — sample-only throttles and dry-run modes are available. they let you evaluate impact without enforcement.
[19:18] [19:50] Diego: going to demo setting a scheduled quota change — switching to night-window permissive burst, applying to project 'B2-staging' — and showing the audit entry created.
[20:05] Lena: small nit: if audit shows a big diff how do we reconcile it for compliance?
[20:11] Diego: all diffs are stored and you can export a signed bundle for the period.
[20:22] [21:00] Ava: ok we're about 20 minutes left — want to surface a couple real-world patterns from other customers. Samir?
[21:07] Samir: one pattern — "latency-first" customers dedicate small pools and force strict concurrency with low token caps; another is "cost-first" who rely on fair-burst and batching with more tolerant tail latency. many hybrid customers tag critical endpoints as latency-first and let background processes be cost-first.
[21:33] Marco: can the Console annotate which tenants are cost vs latency? we'd like an inventory view.
[21:38] Diego: yes we have a tag-based inventory and you can create views by tag.
[21:45] [22:10] Priya: about data retention — how long are audit events kept by default?
[22:14] Ava: hosted defaults to 90 days; private deployments you control retention. extended retention is an add-on.
[22:24] [22:50] Samir: quick demo of SLA fallback — if latency SLO breached we can route to a simpler model or lower-token variant automatically. this is configured via a route policy.
[23:10] Lena: how do we score quality regressions if we change to a lower-quality model?
[23:15] Diego: Optimize ties model changes to evals; you can set quality gates so a rollout won't proceed if eval metrics degrade beyond threshold.
[23:30] [24:00] Ava: alright let's capture concerns — Priya: compliance and audit; Marco: exact RPS and pilot infra; Lena: guardrails for real-time routes.
[24:12] Priya: yes and also key rotation policy and who has power to change quotas.
[24:20] [25:00] Samir: quick note on CLI/SDK — we have SDKs with read/write quota apis so platform automation can update tokens or query remaining budget programmatically.
[25:13] Marco: how long does it take to deploy a new quota policy across all pods? near real-time?
[25:18] Samir: the control plane pushes updates and runtimes apply in around 10–30s depending on size of cluster; it's near-real-time.
[25:28] [26:00] Diego: showing a small demo of subkey issuance — creating subkeys per tenant and attaching soft-limits. you'll see they show up in the inventory.
[26:15] Jonas: if we have thousands of tenants can subkey overhead be high?
[26:20] Samir: we support hierarchical keys and bulk key operations; scale has been tested into many thousands.
[26:33] [27:00] Marco: another operational ask — we'd like to label certain tenants as 'internal' to never be throttled. is that possible?
[27:06] Samir: yes, you can mark protected tenants and set whitelist rules; protected tenants still count against org spend unless you carve separate billing keys.
[27:20] [27:40] Ava: demo is winding up — last thing: we want to show you how Optimize recommends quota profiles based on traffic.
[27:47] Diego: launching a short analysis... it identified two routes that could be moved to q4_0 quant and save ~27% cost with minor quality impact. it also suggested 50ms batching for a mid-size prompt set.
[28:05] Lena: interesting. can you annotate which prompts are risk for quantization?
[28:09] Diego: yes it lists sample prompts that had >X% divergence; those stay on higher fidelity.
[28:20] [29:00] Priya: final compliance question — is there an immutable audit trail for quota changes? we need non-repudiation.
[29:07] Ava: we support signed audit exports and can integrate with your existing archive process.
[29:20] [29:50] Marco: ok let's sync on timing for pilot kickoff. I can get infra people ready week of 3/30.
[29:57] Ava: perfect, we'll target week of 3/30. Samir and Diego will do the pilot setup.
[30:05] [30:30] Samir: on the technical checklist: we need anonymized request traces, desired SLOs, target routes, and which tenants to include in sticky routing tests.
[30:40] Jonas: I'll coordinate sample prompt sets with product.
[30:44] [31:10] Diego: adding note — for private VPC pilot we'll need network peering details; for hosted pilot we need IP allowlist.
[31:20] Priya: can we do an initial dry-run of throttling in a non-prod mirror first?
[31:25] Samir: yes, dry-run mode is ideal and we recommend it before enforcement.
[31:33] [32:00] Ava: cool — recap of next steps coming up in the follow-up email. anything else?
[32:06] Lena: just one more on pricing: if we end up with dedicated capacity long-term, what's the typical commit size?
[32:12] Ava: varies; typical is 4–16 GPU pool depending on throughput — we'll send an estimate for a few tiers.
[32:23] Marco: ok thanks — this was useful.
[32:27] [33:00] Diego: showing terminal again — example curl with the headers and sample response sizes. you may see some weird transcription like 'kayvee' as Samir said.
[33:10] [33:45] Samir: final note — we'll prepare a short benchmark plan for the pilot and share it.
[33:50] Ava: great. thanks everyone for your time. we'll send follow-up with SOC2, SAML examples, pilot checklist, and pricing options.
[34:02] [34:30] Lena: thanks, bye.
[34:34] Marco: bye.
